title: The DICTO OG Family: Four Steps Up and Four Down
main: Eight new icosahedral solids grown outward and inward from the DICTO Ogdoecontahedron by one rule and its reverse, exact in ℚ(√5), with the shells between them and where the nesting breaks

title: The DICTO OG Family on Every Stacking
main: Two short rules, the twin rule and the fit rule, place the Ogdoecontahedron and its family in the tetrahedral–octahedral honeycomb stacked in any order, with one exact kit for the octet, the gyrated octet, the classical polytypes and a Fibonacci stacking that never repeats

title: The DICTO Jewel
main: Euclid's dodecahedron carved by its neighbours' stella octangulas: an exact solid with twelve Penrose windows, its lattice, the DICTO Jewel-Tetra, Jewel-Octa and Jewel-Rhombi and how they fill space, and the DICTO Hexa and Hexa-Key, all exact

title: The DICTO Sunstar
main: Regular dodecahedra and Dogstars fill space: the Dogstar as an exact stellation, the Star Chain Reaction, the DICTO Sunstar-Tetra, Sunstar-Octa and Sunstar-Rhombi, and the DICTO Sunstar-Hexa and Sunstar-Hexa-Key, all exact; the twin of the DICTO Jewel

title: DICTO Kyushindo Cores
main: Towers and spires round exact cores in Fibonacci beats: the DICTO Cleo Towers, the DICTO Polar Cleo Towers, the OG core of 80 Aktis, the OTT core of 38 rays (Oktaktis, Triaktis and Tetraktis), and the OG turned out

title: Aristotle's Pyramid
main: Main theorem. A non-empty set U of the five face pyramids fills space if and only if U is {C}, {T, O} or {C, T, O}: the cube's pyramid alone, the tetrahedron's and the octahedron's pyramids together, or both of these. More precisely, in every tiling of space by copies of face pyramids, (a) no tile is a D or an I, and (b) T tiles occur if and only if O tiles occur.

title: The Reuleaux Platonic Solids
main: Main theorem. Let S be a Platonic solid of diameter 1 and B its body. (i) Every width of B is at least 1, and the width along the line through any two corners at distance 1 is exactly 1. (ii) If S is a cube, octahedron, dodecahedron or icosahedron, with circumradius ½ and inradius r, then along the axis through its centre and a face centre the width of B is exactly 2√(3/4 + r²) − 2r.
others: Conjecture 1 (the largest width). For the cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron the largest width of B is the face-axis width of the main theorem; for the tetrahedron it is √3 − √2/2, along the edge-midpoint axis. For the tetrahedron √3 − √2/2 is the value commonly quoted as the Reuleaux tetrahedron's largest width (not in the library sources checked), so the conjecture is new only for the other four bodies.

title: Every Mix of the Platonic Solids Fills Space
main: Main theorem. Every one of the 31 mixes fills space with connectors from the kit K = {P, Q, Q′, A, S, X, Y} of Table 1. The tiling can be chosen as a stack of slabs between parallel planes, each slab periodic along its planes, and the stack periodic across them.

title: The Golden Split: Icosahedra, Unborns and AXE Become Two Convex Space-Fillers
main: Main theorem (the golden split). At t = 1/φ: (a) the Icosaxes I(1/φ) is convex: it is the truncated octahedron with corners all permutations of (±½, ±φ/2, 0), with 8 hexagons and 6 squares; (b) the Unborn Axes U(1/φ) is convex: it is the truncated octahedron with corners c + all permutations of (±1/(2φ), ±φ/2, 0), with 8 hexagons and 6 squares; (c) both have full octahedral symmetry; all 16 hexagons are congruent, equiangular (120°), with sides alternately 1/√2 and 1/(φ√2); the squares of the Icosaxes have side 1/√2, those of the Unborn Axes 1/(φ√2); (d) their volumes are 1 + 2√5/3 and 1 + √5/3, together φ³; (e) the 12 apices of the Icosaxes are the corners of the mirror image of its icosahedron in the plane x = y through its centre, and the 12 apices of the Unborn Axes those of the mirror image of its Unborn in the plane x = y through c; (f) Icosaxes at the points of φℤ³ and Unborn Axes at the cube centres fill space face to face: Icosaxes meet Icosaxes on their squares, Unborn Axes meet Unborn Axes on theirs, and the two meet each other on the hexagons.
others: Theorem 2 (uniqueness). Cut each AXE from any point p inside it, possibly different for different AXEs, and give its four pyramids to their neighbours as before. If the padded icosahedra and the padded Unborns are all convex, then every AXE is cut at its golden point p(1/φ). In particular, for cut points p(t) on the axis (0 ≤ t ≤ 1) the padded icosahedron I(t) is not convex for t > 1/φ and the padded Unborn U(t) is not convex for t < 1/φ.

Theorem 3 (Lotus Jewel Axes and Dodecaxes). In the Lotus Jewel network, the golden split gives the Lotus Jewel Axes J + 12 pyramids, which is the Icosaxes with its 8 Tricaps removed, and the Dodecaxes D + 12 pyramids, which is the Unborn Axes with 8 Tricaps added. Their volumes are exactly √5 and 2. Each Tricap stands on a hexagon shared by an Icosaxes and an Unborn Axes; for every choice of giving each Tricap to the one or the other, the resulting pieces fill space.

Theorem 4 (factor x). For x > 0 let T(x) be the semi-uniform truncated octahedron [4], written as Koca’s orbit [1, eq. 49]: the convex hull of all permutations of (±(1 + x), ±x, 0), scaled so that its squares lie at distance L/2 from its centre. Then for every x > 0, copies of T(x) at the points of Lℤ³ and copies of T(1/x) at the cube centres (L/2)(1, 1, 1) + Lℤ³ fill space face to face. Their volumes add to L³. At x = 1 both are the uniform truncated octahedron (Kelvin’s cell); at x = τ they are the Icosaxes and the Unborn Axes (L = φ).

title: The Polyhedral Stretching Theorem
main: The Polyhedral Stretching Theorem. Let P be a convex polyhedron whose edges all have length 1, and slide it a distance 1 along a direction u. The swept shape (the convex hull of P and P moved by u) has every edge of length 1 unless u is parallel to an edge of P. Its faces are: each face of P not parallel to u, kept whole (one copy, at the end it faces); each n-sided face parallel to u, stretched into an (n+2)-gon, with one side fewer for each of its edges parallel to u; and one parallelogram for every edge of P's outline seen along u, a rhombus when the slide is 1.

title: One Move Each: Classical Cut-and-Glue Space-Fillers Built Exactly
main: Main theorem. Each solid in Table 1 is obtained exactly by the Kaleidohedra move in its row: the shear, then the equal-edged cell (where stated), then the stretch (where stated). It tiles space by translations of the moved lattice, its corners lie in the stated number field, and it is congruent, by an exact corner-matching test, to the classical construction in the last column. Its faces, symmetry and volume are as stated (all at edge 1, except where the edge is given).
others: Theorem 2 (three free directions). Let Z = Z(h 1 , …, h 4 ) be an RD-type cell with Σ μ i h i = 0, all μ i > 0, and let u be a direction not parallel to any h i . Then Z + [0, s·u] (s > 0) is a parallelohedron if and only if u is parallel to one of the three vectors u ij|kl = μ i h i + μ j h j = −(μ k h k + μ l h l ), one for each way of splitting the four vectors into two pairs; the line of u ij|kl is where the plane of h i , h j meets the plane of h k , h l . For each of them, and every s > 0, it is an elongated dodecahedron (18 corners, 28 edges, 12 faces).

Proposition 3. (a) With the FCC sliders a = b = c, α = β = 60° and γ moved from 60° to 36° (cos γ = φ/2), Cell = 1 gives the Bilinski dodecahedron B exactly; its lattice has Gram matrix proportional to [[1, φ/2, ½], [φ/2, 1, ½], [½, ½, 1]]. (b) Cell = 1 is needed: at Cell = 0 the same sliders give a linear image of Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron, which is not B. (c) B is congruent to T with any two of its six zones deleted, for all 15 pairs, and is glued exactly from four golden rhombohedra, two acute and two obtuse, in two ways.

title: The Delian Bond: Samson, Delilah and the Octet Between Kepler's Rhombic Dodecahedron and the Cube
main: Main theorem. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 cut every double cone B F by the plane parallel to F through the point c T + t(c O − c T ), and let T(t) be the union of the 4 parts next to a tetrahedron's centre and O(t) the union of the 8 parts next to an octahedron's centre. Then the pieces T(t) and O(t) fill space face to face, both are convex, and: (a) for 0 < t ≤ 1/3, T(t) is the regular tetrahedron of edge 3t, volume 27t³·V T , and O(t) is the rhombic dodecahedron with its 8 three-fold corners cut off by planes parallel to the octahedron's faces (8 triangles and 12 hexagons for t < 1/3), volume (6 − 54t³)·V T ; (b) for 1/3 ≤ t < 1, with a = 3(1 − t)/2, O(t) is the regular octahedron of edge a, volume 4a³·V T , and T(t) is the cube with its 4 corners at octahedron centres cut off (4 triangles and 6 hexagons for t > 1/3), volume (3 − 2a³)·V T ; (c) at t = 0 the pieces are the rhombic dodecahedra alone, at t = 1/3 the octet, at t = 1 the cubes alone.
others: Theorem 2. (a) At t = (2√6 − 3)/15 every edge of the filling, of the tetrahedra and of the cut rhombic dodecahedra alike, has length (2√6 − 3)/5. (b) At t = 5/3 − (2/3)√2 every edge, of the cut cubes and of the octahedra alike, has length √2 − 1. (c) At t = 1 − ∛6/3 the tetrahedron pieces and the octahedron pieces each fill exactly half of space. (d) For no t is a hexagon regular.

Theorem 3 (the Delian bond). T(t) and O(t) have equal volume at exactly one position, t D = 1 − (2/3)·2 −1/3 . There Samson , the cut cube T(t D ), and Delilah , the octahedron O(t D ), both have volume √2/6 = 2V T = V O /2: Samson twice the octet's tetrahedron and Delilah half the octet's octahedron. Delilah is the octet's octahedron shrunk by the factor 2 −1/3 , so her edge is 1/∛2; Samson's edges are 1/∛2 (his triangles, which are Delilah's faces) and (1 − 2 −1/3 )/√2.

title: The Web of Bonds: How the DICTONIC Bonds Hand Over
main: Main theorem. (i) For every x ∈ [0, ∞] the golden network is the power diagram of the body-centred cubic sites B ∪ S with w B − w S = (φ²/4)(x − 1)/(x + 1) = (L/2)²(2s − 1). For every t ∈ [0, 1] the Delian network is the power diagram of Q ∪ O with w Q − w O = (3/8)(2t − 1). At t = 0 the Q cells are single points, at t = 1 the O cells are single points. (ii) The web of bonds is the 1-skeleton of the dual regular subdivision, and the bond faces and their areas are those of Table 1. (iii) Golden: gradual hand-over. For 0 < x < ∞ all three bond types are present and the face lattice is constant. Big–big rises strictly from 0 and small–small falls strictly to 0; their ratio is x², the diagonals of the two square faces (sL and (1 − s)L) add up to the lattice spacing φ, and the two areas are equal only at x = 1. The whole picture is symmetric under x ↔ 1/x. Delian: hand-over at the octet. Oct–tet is present exactly on (0, 1), oct–oct exactly on [0, 1/3), tet–tet exactly on (1/3, 1]. t = 1/3 is the only parameter at which both pieces exist and every face is of one bond type (there the web is bipartite). The ends t = 0 and t = 1 carry one bond type only because one piece has shrunk to a point. The golden loop never has a single bond type: at x = 0 there are two (big–small and small–small), at x = ∞ two (big–small and big–big).
others: Theorem 2 (the balls). (a) The radical tessellation of a packing of balls (c i , r i ) is the power diagram with w i = r i ² + C, for any common constant C; a power diagram therefore fixes the radii only up to r i ² → r i ² + C. (b) The golden sites are the caesium chloride structure (B2, Wyckoff 1a and 1b, lattice constant a = φ in app units); the Delian sites, shifted by (1, 0, 0)/√2, are the fluorite structure (C1: the oct sites on the face-centred cubic 4a, the tet sites on 8c, all the tetrahedral holes; a = √2). (c) If unlike neighbours touch, the radius ratio is ρ = r small /r big = (x + 2)/(2x + 1) = (2 − s)/(1 + s) on the golden loop and ρ = r tet-site /r oct-site = t/(1 − t) on the Delian loop; so t is exactly the share of the unlike bond length taken by the tet-site ball. (d) The touching window (unlike balls touching, like balls not overlapping) is x ∈ [(√3 − 1)/2, √3 + 1], ρ ∈ [√3 − 1, (√3 + 1)/2] on the golden loop, and t ∈ [1 − √(2/3), 1/√3], ρ ∈ [√(3/2) − 1, (√3 + 1)/2] on the Delian loop. Its ends are Pauling's radius-ratio limits [9] and their reciprocals: √3 − 1 ≈ 0.732 for 8-coordination (golden lower end; Delian upper end as 1/(√3 − 1) = (√3 + 1)/2), and √(3/2) − 1 ≈ 0.225 for 4-coordination (Delian lower end). (e) Without the touching condition, some non-overlapping ball packing realises every x ∈ [0, ∞], but only the t ∈ [1/6, 2/3].

title: The Global Web of Bonds: How Bonds Hand Over Across Crystal Networks
main: Main theorem (the census). Let N be one of the ten two-kind networks of Table 1, with λ = w A − w B . (i) Range. Both kinds have cells of positive volume exactly for λ in the open interval of Table 2. At its lower end every A cell is a single point, at its upper end every B cell is. (ii) Flips. The face lattice of the power diagram is constant on each open interval between consecutive values in the "flips" column of Table 2, and differs on the two sides of each of them. All flips are rational. Appendix C lists, for every interval and every stop, the face vector of every cell and its bonds by neighbour kind. (iii) Bond lives. Each bond type is present exactly on the single interval of Table 2 (a bracket marks an end included). In particular, in all ten networks the unlike bond is present on the whole open range and only there. (iv) Switch points. A switch point exists exactly in four networks: λ = 0 in square + centres, λ = −1/2 in honeycomb + centres, λ = 0 in rock salt and λ = −1/8 in fluorite. There the dual cells are squares (2 corner + 2 centre sites), rhombi (2 honeycomb + 2 centre sites), cubes (4 Na + 4 Cl) and rhombic dodecahedra (6 oct + 8 tet), and every piece has only unlike bonds: 4 and 4; 3 per honeycomb piece and 6 per centre piece; 6 and 6; 8 per oct piece and 4 per tet piece. In the other six networks no value of λ in the range, flip or not, has only unlike bonds. (v) Three kinds. For the perovskite sites, all three kinds have cells of positive volume exactly on the open rectangle −2 < λ < 2, −1 < μ < 1 (its closure has area 8). It is cut by the three straight walls λ = 0, λ + 2μ = 0 and λ + μ = 1 into five chambers of constant face lattice. Each wall is the birth or death line of exactly one bond type: A–A is present for λ > 0, A–B for λ + 2μ > 0, X–X for λ + μ < 1. A–X and B–X are present in every chamber, B–B in none, and no point of the open rectangle (chamber, wall or corner) has only unlike bonds.
others: Proposition 1 (the unlike bond can never break). In any face-to-face tiling of space by convex cells of two kinds A and B (periodic or not, locally finite), if both kinds have cells of positive volume then some A cell and some B cell share a facet. Hence, in every two-kind network, the unlike bond is present at every parameter at which both kinds have cells. With three or more kinds, every kind shares a facet with some cell of another kind: each kind keeps some unlike bond, but not necessarily with every other kind.

title: One Turn Is a Gnomon: the Golden Cycle Step by Step, and the Polar of the Keyed Pair
main: Theorem A (the classical gnomon of the golden cycle; exact, computer-verified in exact arithmetic). Let the twelve stations be as in Table 2, repeated in every turn at scale φ 3m . (i) Among the twelve stations exactly one pair is similar: I and I·φ³, with linear ratio φ³ = 2 + √5 (volume ratio φ⁹). (ii) Hence the whole turn, the region between I and I·φ³, is a classical gnomon of I, a solid gnomon: added to I it makes a whole similar to I. (iii) No single step, and no run of consecutive steps shorter than a whole turn, is a classical gnomon: the new whole is never similar to the station it was added to. In particular no step k → k + 1 is a gnomon of station k. (iv) In the turn that starts at I, the last step, M → I·φ³, is the only step whose new whole is similar to an earlier station; it is the step that closes the gnomon of the turn. The new wholes of steps 1–10 are similar to no other station of the turn. (v) In the endless cycle every station is similar to the same station one turn (eleven steps) earlier and to no other earlier station; so every whole turn, from whichever station it starts, is a classical gnomon of that station, and nothing shorter is.
others: Corollary A (volumes; exact, computer-verified in exact arithmetic, with the algebraic reasons in the proof). With the volumes of Table 2: (i) the cycle opens by doubling: Cleo star = 2·I, the first step adds one I; (ii) it closes by φ: M = φ⁸·I, so I·φ³ = φ⁹·I = φ·M, and the last step adds φ⁷·I; (iii) RT = 81·I/φ², hence M/RT = φ¹⁰/81 and I·φ³/RT = φ¹¹/81; (iv) of the 66 ratios V j /V i (i < j) exactly ten are of the form q·φ k with q rational and k an integer, all among I, Cleo star, RT, M and I·φ³; (v) of the eleven added volumes exactly four are of the form q·φ k ·I, those of steps 1, 6, 7 and 11: I, (3/4)φ⁻²·I, 18φ⁻⁴·I and φ⁷·I (Table 3). They add up to (φ⁹ − 1)·I.

Theorem B (hull and remainder; exact, with a hand proof of (i)–(iii) and computer-verified in exact arithmetic). Take polars in the unit sphere about each piece's own centre, and measure pyramid heights in half cube edges. (i) For every x > 0 the polar of T(x) is a cube with a square pyramid of height x/(1 + x) on each face, and the polar of its partner T(1/x) one with height 1/(1 + x). The two heights add up to 1, the height of the pyramids that turn a cube into Kepler's rhombic dodecahedron [10]. (ii) For the golden pair: the polar of the Icosaxes has pyramids of height 1/φ and that of the Unborn Axes of height 1/φ², and 1/φ + 1/φ² = 1. Both polars have their apexes at distance 2/φ from the centre; their cube corners lie at 2√3/φ² and 2√3/√5. (iii) In DICTO's hull-and-remainder reading the Lotus Jewel Axes is the polar of (ii) for the Icosaxes with the eight Tricaps as remainder, and the Dodecaxes that of the Unborn Axes with the same eight Tricaps as remainder. (iv) Taken face by face about the one centre, the three walls of each dent of the Lotus Jewel Axes have their poles at distance √(10 − 2√5) = 4 sin 36° ≈ 2.351, against 2√3/φ² ≈ 1.323 for the hexagon the dent sits in, and ≈ 37.38° away from its direction.

title: David and Goliath: Jessen's Icosahedron and the Tetrahedron in the A15 Weight Walk
main: Main theorem (David and Goliath). In A15 at λ = 3/4: (i) the power cell of the Si site at the origin is Goliath , the convex hull of the 12 points (0, ±1/2, ±1), (±1, 0, ±1/2), (±1/2, ±1, 0); it is a convex icosahedron with 20 triangular faces, 12 corners all of degree 5 and 30 edges, 6 of length 1 and 24 of length √(3/2); each of its 8 equilateral faces is shared with a neighbouring Goliath (around the Si site at squared distance 3), each of its 12 isosceles faces with a David (around the Cr site at squared distance 5/4); its volume is 7/2; (ii) the power cell of the Cr site (1/2, 0, 1) is David , the tetrahedron with corners (0, ±1/2, 1), (1, 0, 1/2), (1, 0, 3/2): a tetragonal disphenoid with its two opposite edges of length 1, its other four of length √(3/2), four congruent isosceles faces, centroid at its Cr site, and volume 1/6; all four faces are shared with Si cells; (iii) every other cell is the image of Goliath or David under a symmetry of the structure, and the tiling has 2 Goliaths and 6 Davids per cubic cell: 2 · 7/2 + 6 · 1/6 = 8, the volume of the cell; (iv) Goliath's corner set is exactly Jessen's corner set scaled by 1/2, so Goliath is the convex hull of Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron (scaled by 1/2).

title: Sonsam and Lahdeli: the Delian Bond on the Twinned Octet, with Ian Dury, Blockhead and Keyed Switch Points
main: Theorem. On the twinned octet the walk has, for −1/8 ≤ λ ≤ 3/8, exactly these stops and pieces: λ = −1/8: the octet's regular octahedra and tetrahedra, twinned. On −1/8 < λ < 5/24 every tetrahedral site has the same cell, a solid of 19 corners with 6 triangles, 3 pentagons, 3 hexagons and one 9-gon, and every octahedral site a solid of 12 corners with 2 triangles and 6 pentagons. Their volumes are equal at exactly one λ, the single root in this stretch of 1536λ³ + 5184λ² − 3384λ + 11 = 0 (λ ≈ 0.0032669570), a cubic with no rational root. There both have volume √2/6: these are Sonsam and Lahdeli . λ = 5/24: the tetrahedral cells are Ian Durys (16 corners: 6 triangles, 3 squares, 4 hexagons; volume 13√2/54) and the octahedral cells are 60° rhombohedra of edge 1/3 (volume √2/54), bonded only to Ian Durys. λ = 3/8: the octahedral cells have shrunk to points; the tetrahedral cells are Blockheads (10 corners: 6 triangles, 3 squares, 1 hexagon; volume √2/4), four per cell. On the cubic octet the walk goes from the octet (λ = −1/8) to cubes (λ = 3/8) with no stop between, and the equal-volume point is λ = 3/8 − ∛4/4, where Samson and Delilah [3] both have volume √2/6.
others: Keying lemma. Let P and Q be pieces of a tiling sharing a face F, and K a solid inside P whose base lies inside F and which touches no other piece. Replacing P, Q by P \ K and Q ∪ K gives again a tiling of space (the pieces are no longer convex, and P \ K and Q ∪ K now meet along F minus the base and along the sides of K, so the tiling is no longer face to face in the strict sense); P \ K and Q ∪ K still meet, and every other contact is unchanged, so the web of bonds is the same. Proof: (P \ K) ∪ (Q ∪ K) = P ∪ Q and the two parts do not overlap; K touches only P and Q, so no other piece or contact changes. □

title: The Rule of Halves: the Holes of Every Close-Packed Stacking
main: Theorem (the rule of halves). For every close-packed stacking and every λ with −11/24 ≤ λ ≤ 3/8: the piece of a tetrahedral hole is congruent to a tetrahedral piece of the pure stacking (cubic if c, hexagonal if h) of the type of its nearest layer: the hole over X, at height (k + ¾)d, is nearest to layer k + 1, the hole over Y to layer k; the piece of an octahedral hole, cut by the horizontal plane through the hole, has a top half congruent to the top half of an octahedral piece of the pure stacking of the type of layer k + 1, and a bottom half congruent to the bottom half of an octahedral piece of the pure stacking of the type of layer k. Corollaries. (i) Up to congruence there are finitely many pieces in all close-packed stackings together: 21 combinatorial kinds, listed in the Appendix with exact volumes. (ii) The volume of an octahedral piece is the mean of the volumes of its cubic and hexagonal parents (or equal to the parent's, when both layers have the same type).

title: From the Octet to Every Stacking: the Web of Bonds
main: How cutting gaps in the right place, and watching which pieces touch, led to one rule for every way of stacking balls

title: The Icosaxes Hexa: Bloom, Bud and Seed
main: Twenty golden truncated octahedra closing round a centre in three golden steps, and the network they make

title: DICTO Janus c/h Pyrochlore
main: The rule of halves of #57 carried to the pyrochlore network, its layers stacked in any order

title: The White Queen 600-cell
main: Lemma (one pattern per gap). Let h₁ < h₂ be two neighbouring vertex heights. At every height strictly between them the slice has the same pattern of faces. Proof. An edge of the 600-cell crosses the cut at height h exactly when its two ends lie on opposite sides of h. No vertex has a height strictly between h₁ and h₂, so as h moves through the gap no vertex changes side, and the same edges cross the cut. Inside the gap each face of the slice is the cross-section of one tetrahedral cell, with its corners at the crossing points on that cell's edges, and two faces share an edge of the slice exactly when their cells share a triangle that is cut. Which cells and triangles are cut, and through which edges, is therefore the same throughout the gap, and so is the pattern of faces. Hence the cuts at the vertex heights and one cut inside each gap give every slice pattern. The lemma is about the pattern only: edge lengths and angles change with the height.
others: Theorem. Exactly twelve of the 62 slice patterns are made only of triangles: eleven at vertex heights and one inside a gap.

title: Spin Ice and Kagome Magnets on Every Stacking
main: Theorem 1. On the pyrochlore network of any close-packed stacking with hexagonality h: (i) there are two sites per atom of the parent network, one quarter in triangular layers and three quarters in kagome layers; (ii) per tetrahedron, h/2 of the corner-sharing pairs are eclipsed (mirror images across the shared corner) and the rest staggered (inversion images).
others: Loop Equality (computed; conjecture for all lengths). On every close-packed stacking, the number of closed non-backtracking loops of each length per site is the same. Computed for all even lengths from 6 to 34 on the five stackings: 24, 48, 480, 3432, 25704, 194256, 1509072, 11820000, …, 27416593190640, identical to the last digit.

Theorem 2. In an A 3 B close-packed stacking with hexagonality h, each A atom lies on 1 + 3(1 − h) kagome planes: always its own layer, and three tilted planes if its layer is cubic, none if it is hexagonal.

title: HexOct: Knitting Crystals
main: Theorem 1 (the slice). For every close-packed stacking: (a) P meets each layer in exactly one ball centre per repeat √3, at s = 0, √3/3, 2√3/3 (0, 1/3, 2/3 of the repeat) for A, B, C; every other ball centre lies at distance 1/2, so those balls touch P at one point only. (b) P is a mirror plane of the stacking. Every tetrahedron that P cuts meets it in an isosceles triangle with sides 1, √3/2, √3/2 (angles 70.53°, 54.74°, 54.74°) whose side 1 is a whole edge joining touching balls of the two layers; every octahedron that P cuts meets it in a rhombus of side √3/2 and angles arccos(1/3) = 70.53° and 109.47°, with two sides in the layer planes. (c) The mid-planes cut each triangle into a small triangle (1/2, √3/4, √3/4) at its tip and a trapezoid (√3/2, √3/4, 1/2, √3/4) at its base, and each rhombus into two congruent parallelograms (√3/2, √3/4): these are the halves of the Rule of Halves, and they tile the slice. (d) In the band of every layer (from the mid-plane below to the mid-plane above) the tetrahedral and the octahedral halves have equal area. So exactly half of the slice is dark and half light, and the blue share is exactly the hexagonality.
others: Theorem 2 (bias placement). Let a chart repeat be 3k stitches and move the knitting k stitches sideways across every gap, to the right when the stacking steps A→B, B→C or C→A and to the left otherwise. Then (a) the ball stitches of every layer fall in the same chart columns; and (b) the step out of a c layer goes the same way as the step into it, and the step out of an h layer goes back: a run of c layers knits as one straight slant, a run of h layers as a zigzag (chevron).

title: Shadows of the Fourth Dimension
main: Main result. The triangle-faced shadows and slices of the 5-, 16-, 24- and 600-cell give deltahedra of two new kinds. (a) Variants that join differently (§4). The 5-cell's edge-first shadow (TBP-5) has the pattern of the triangular bipyramid J12 with unequal edges, and three copies of it close face to face round an edge. The 16-cell's edge-first shadow (OCT-16) has the pattern of the octahedron with unequal edges, and it fills space on its own. (b) Equal-edged solids from the 600-cell (§5, §6). Four of the 600-cell's shadows and slices can be rebuilt exactly with every edge the same length, keeping their pattern of triangles: the vertex-first shadow (42 vertices, 80 triangles) as a 12-dented icosahedron; the slices at the dodecahedron height (32 vertices, 60 triangles) as the excavated and the augmented dodecahedron; the outer edge-first slices (17 vertices, 30 triangles) as Shadow-17, two J11 glued on their pentagons; and the 48-vertex cell-first slice (92 triangles) as Slice-48, with tetrahedral symmetry. All four forms are non-convex.
others: Proposition 1. No shadow, layer or slice of the 5-, 16-, 24- or 600-cell along the four main directions is a regular deltahedron, except copies of the solid's own cells and vertex figures. Among the others, the only patterns of a convex deltahedron that occur are those of the triangular bipyramid and the octahedron, each with unequal edges.

Proposition 2. A bipyramid over an n-gon with all edges equal exists only for n ≤ 5: for n ≥ 6 the equilateral apex would lie in the plane of the polygon or the solid would cross itself. So the hexagonal and decagonal bipyramid patterns of the 16- and 600-cell have no equilateral form.

Slice-48 (placeholder name). The 48-vertex cell-first slice of the 600-cell has exactly one equilateral form with its tetrahedral symmetry Td: 48 vertices (12 of degree 8, 36 of degree 5), 138 equal edges and 92 triangles. It is not convex: 24 of its vertices lie on its hull, and its dihedral angles are 81.75°, 130.98°, 135.83°, 143.83°, 191.03°, 197.94°, 216.17° and 243.20°. At edge length 1, its nearest non-adjacent parts are 0.069 apart; the embedding was confirmed with exact orientation tests on 85-digit rational coordinates.

title: DICTO Vacuus Solids
main: Proposition 1 (when the Vacuus exists). If O lies strictly on the inner side of every face plane of P, the centre pyramids fill P without overlap. If O lies on or beyond some face plane, they do not.
others: Definition (DICTO Vacuus). The DICTO Vacuus of P is the union of its fins, one per edge. It is built in two forms: SHEETS , the fins as thin plates; and STRUTS , one rod from O to every corner, with the solid's edges (the fins' outer sides) as an option. The DICTO Vacuus Solids are the solids taken in these forms.
Theorem (polar law). Let δ(e) be the dihedral angle of P at the edge e, and φ f (v) the face angle of the face f at the corner v. Then:

Proposition 2 (the Star law). Let P satisfy Proposition 1 and let Star(P) be P together with its turned-out centre pyramids. (a) The volume of Star(P) is exactly twice that of P. (b) At an edge of P with dihedral angle δ, the dihedral angle of Star(P) is 2δ. (c) The surface of Star(P) is the Vacuus of P reflected, fin by fin, in the face planes.

title: The Hexagonality Law and the Fibonacci Stacking
main: Theorem. In the Fibonacci stacking (i) the share of hexagonal layers is h = 1/φ² = (3 − √5)/2; (ii) no two hexagonal layers are neighbours; (iii) among the pairs of neighbouring layers, cubic–cubic has frequency 1/φ³, cubic–hexagonal and hexagonal–cubic 1/φ² each, hexagonal–hexagonal 0. (iv) For every kind of piece to which the Hexagonality Law applies, the average volume per layer is exactly V(cc) + (V(hh) − V(cc))(3 − √5)/2.
others: Result. On the 15-, 16- and 26-layer Fibonacci approximants, every role of the Laves phases, the foot atom M0 included, keeps the Hexagonality Law exactly: 90 of 90 tests. The 26-layer approximant (hexagonality 5/13 ≈ 0.385) is the closest to the golden 1/φ² computed so far.

title: Random Stackings and Stacking Faults
main: Theorem 1. Let a role satisfy the Swap Rule. For any sequence of N consecutive layers of any stacking, periodic or not, the total volume T of that role's pieces in the N − 1 gaps between them satisfies |T − (n c F(c, c) + n h F(h, h))| ≤ 2·max|f| + 2·max|g|, where n c , n h count the cubic and hexagonal layers. Hence, in any stacking whose share of hexagonal layers tends to h, the average volume per layer tends to F(c, c) + h·(F(h, h) − F(c, c)), whatever the order of the layers and whatever the correlations between them.
others: Theorem 2. Let a role satisfy the Swap Rule. Compared with a perfect crystal of the same number of layers, a stacking fault that changes Δ layers from cubic to hexagonal (Δ < 0: from hexagonal to cubic) changes the total volume of that role's pieces by exactly Δ·(F(h, h) − F(c, c)).

Result. On all 13 non-pure close-packed stackings up to eight layers, in all five windows of λ, every role of the Laves phases, the foot atom M0 included, totals exactly n c F(c, c) + n h F(h, h): 390 of 390 exact tests.

title: The Hexagonality Law in Real Materials II
main: Proposition. If a crystal's volume per pair follows the law's form (a straight line in the hexagonality, J 2 V = J 3 V = 0), then at first order pressure changes only J 1 : it shifts the balance between cubic and hexagonal layers, adds the same amount per hexagonal layer to every stacking, keeps the fault ratios intrinsic : extrinsic : twin of its own contribution at 2 : 2 : 1, and leaves J 2 and J 3 , which order the longer stackings among themselves, unchanged.

title: The Hexagonality Law in Real Materials III
main: Theorem. Per ball, in any close-packed stacking: (i) the pairs of tetrahedral holes sharing a face number h; (ii) the pairs of octahedral holes sharing a face number h. Consequently (iii) if two hydrogen atoms cannot occupy one face-sharing tetrahedral pair, at most 2 − h tetrahedral sites per ball can be filled, and (iv) a hydride MH x with its hydrogen in tetrahedral sites needs local hexagonality h ≤ 2 − x.
others: Proposition. In the layer model, ρΔG = 2(J 1 + J 3 ) and 2σ = 4J 2 . So σ = 0 exactly when the second-neighbour coupling vanishes, and σ measures how far a material's faults are from the law.

title: The Hexagonality Law in Real Materials IV
main: Theorem. (i) In a perovskite ABO 3 built of close-packed AO 3 layers with B in the octahedra formed by oxygen alone, each B octahedron shares a face with 2h neighbours and a corner with 6(1 − h) neighbours, for any stacking. (ii) In a layered oxide LiMO 2 (oxygen layers in pairs around the M layers, lithium in the gaps), the face-sharing lithium–metal pairs number 2h per lithium site; a gap bounded by two cubic layers (O3 type) has none, a gap bounded by two hexagonal layers (O1 type) has two, a mixed gap (O2 type) has one.
others: Proposition (lithium bound). If lithium occupies only gaps in which it shares no face with a metal octahedron, then x ≤ 1 − h gap , where h gap is the share of O1-type gaps. All stable phases in Motohashi et al.'s series obey it: O3 (h gap = 0, x ≤ 1), H1-3 (1/2, x = 0.12), O1 (1, x = 0).

title: The Hexagonality Law in Real Materials V
main: Theorem. In a tetrahedral network on any close-packed stacking, per atom: (i) the eclipsed bonds number h/2 (all other bonds are staggered); (ii) the eclipsed third-neighbour pairs number 3h/2, at 5/3 of the bond length (staggered third neighbours lie at 1.915 and 2.517 bond lengths).
others: Prediction. To the extent that the law holds for ice, stacking-disordered ice of cubicity Φ releases 37.7 Φ J/mol on turning hexagonal, and its excess vapour pressure over hexagonal ice is Φ times that of cubic ice. The eclipsed hydrogen bonds number (1 − Φ)/2 per molecule.

title: Real Polytypes and the Hexagonality Law
main: Proposition. (i) A property X of the polytypes 3C, 6H, 4H and 2H is a straight line in h, X = s·h, exactly when J 2 = J 3 = 0 (and then J 1 = s/2). (ii) For such a property the stacking faults of a cubic crystal stand X(ISF) : X(ESF) : X(TSF) = 2 : 2 : 1, where, in the same model, X(ISF) = 4(J 1 + J 2 + J 3 ), X(ESF) = 4(J 1 + 2J 2 + 2J 3 ) and X(TSF) = 2(J 1 + 2J 2 + 3J 3 ).

title: The Red Queen 120-cell
main: Theorem. In perspective from just beyond the far side, along a corner or along a cell centre:
others: Atlas. The Red Queen has 124 slice patterns : 31 corner-first (faces of 3 to 8 sides, largest 108 vertices), 45 edge-first (3 to 9, the only nine-sided faces, largest 114), 33 pentagon-first (3 to 8 and 10, largest 120 vertices and 62 faces) and 15 cell-first (faces of 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 sides, largest 120 vertices).

title: The Swap Rule in Crystals
main: Theorem. In each of the four families, on every close-packed stacking of up to six layers (all of them, up to symmetry; odd ones doubled for CdCl₂/CdI₂) and at every weight λ of its range, every piece has its volume fixed by the layers round its gap (four layers; six for the Laves foot atom), and

title: The Swap Rule
main: Theorem. Let s ≥ ½. Put λ₋(c) = −¼ − s/8, λ₋(h) = −⅓ − s/8 and U(s) = min(⅓ + s/24, 3s/8). In every close-packed stacking, periodic or not, take any hole piece of a gap whose lower layer has type t and upper layer type t′, at any λ with max(λ₋(t), λ₋(t′)) ≤ λ ≤ U(s). Cut it by the horizontal mid-plane of its gap. The part below is congruent to the lower half of the piece of the same kind in the pure stacking of type t, and the part above to the upper half of that piece in the pure stacking of type t′. This holds for all three kinds of hole piece.
others: Theorem 2. For ¼ ≤ s < ½ and every λ up to 3s/8, in every close-packed stacking, each hole piece has volume V(t|t′) = A(t) + B(t′): one term fixed by the lower layer's type, one by the upper layer's. Hence the Swap Rule V(c|h) + V(h|c) = V(c|c) + V(h|h) holds for every s ≥ ¼. The bound ¼ is exact.

title: The Focus
main: Theorem (Hexagonality Law). Let a role have, in the gap between layers of types x (below) and y (above), a piece of volume F(x, y), the same in every stacking. Then the following are equivalent: (i) the Swap Rule F(c, h) + F(h, c) = F(c, c) + F(h, h); (ii) in every stacking, the total volume of the role over one period is T = n c ·F(c, c) + n h ·F(h, h). So each layer holds, in every stacking, exactly what it holds in the pure stacking of its own type, and the total per layer is the straight line F(c, c) + (n h /n)·(F(h, h) − F(c, c)) in the hexagonality.
